target_customer: Software developers (Ruby and JavaScript first) who read and use open source code
problem: Developers lack questions, comments and documentation attached to the exact code they use.
business_model: Free community product with paid plans; it stopped charging in 2016
product_category: Developer tools, code annotation and reference

founders.name: Tim Robertson
founders.background_notes: Background not stated in YC page or VentureBeat.

founders.name: Montana Low
founders.background_notes: Left in 2015 to join Instacart, per VentureBeat.

exit.reason: CEO Tim Robertson said on 2016-12-21 the company never found a sustainable business model to cover the high cost of running the site.

technical_complexity.rationale: Indexing the source of every version of every Ruby Gem and later JavaScript packages, with annotations and a leaderboard, was substantial for two people.

defensibility.rationale: Value depended on community contributions, but there was little lock in and the code index itself was copyable.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent bought or copied it as far as sources show. It shut down on January 31, 2017.

market_need_then: TechCrunch in January 2015 reported about 7,000 sign ups within weeks, and YC's launch post compared the idea to Genius annotations. Developers depended on it, per the shutdown post.

identity.voice_and_tone: Developer community tone: sticky notes for code, a code reference maintained by and for programmers

branding.community_and_virality: A user leaderboard to credit contributors, and a Hacker News relaunch post in 2016. Press framed it as Rap Genius for code.

brand_strength.rationale: Some developer awareness and a clear tagline, but no evidence of a durable brand.

pivots.from: Ruby and JavaScript package source reference with Q and A
pivots.to: Language agnostic universal code reference focused on code review, depending only on git
pivots.why: Described in the founder's 2016 Hacker News relaunch post; reason not detailed in sources opened.

outcome_analysis: Omniref launched in December 2014 with about 7,000 sign ups in weeks and joined YC in Winter 2015. The CTO left for Instacart in 2015, the company stopped charging in 2016, tried a relaunch around code review, and the CEO announced on December 21, 2016 that high running costs and no sustainable business model meant closing on January 31, 2017.
notes: omniref.com returned HTTP 503 from this session, consistent with the site having closed in 2017. The $120K round rests on CB Insights alone and is probably YC's standard deal. VentureBeat does not state funding. The YC launch post names only Genius as a comparable product, which is an inspiration and not a competitor, so the competitor list is empty. The 2016 pivot is from a search result for a Hacker News post, not opened. No founder education or prior employers were found.
